entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.1-Prov.4.4">Pro 4:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> He now confirms and explains the command to duty which he has placed at the beginning of the whole (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>). This he does by his own example, for he relates from the history of his own youth, to the circle of disciples by whom he sees himself surrounded, what good doctrine his parents had taught him regarding the way of life: 1 Hear, ye sons, the instruction of a father,    And attend that ye may gain understanding; 2 For I give to you good doctrine,    Forsake not my direction! 3 For I was a son to my father,    A tender and only (son) in the sight of my mother. 4 And he instructed me, and said to me:    “Let thine heart hold fast my words:    Observe my commandments and live!” <div eID="gen10664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> That בּנים in the address comes here into the place of בּני, hitherto used, externally denotes that בני in the progress of these discourses finds another application: the poet himself is so addressed by his father. Intentionally he does not say אביכם (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>): he does not mean the father of each individual among those addressed, but himself, who is a father in his relation to them as his disciples; and as he manifests towards them fatherly love, so also he can lay claim to paternal authority over them. לדעת is rightly vocalized, not לדעת. The words do not give the object of attention, but the design, the aim. The combination of ideas in דּעת בּינה (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.2">Pro 1:2</reference>), which appears to us singular, loses its strangeness when we remember that דעת means, according to its etymon, deposition or reception into the conscience and life. Regarding לקח, apprehension, reception, lesson = doctrine, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 1:5. נתתּי is the perf., which denotes as fixed and finished what is just now being done, Gesenius, §126, 4. עזב is here synonym of נטשׁ, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.8">Pro 1:8</reference>, and the contrary of שׁמר, Pro 28:4. The relative <hi type="italic">factum</hi> in the perfect, designating the circumstances under which the event happened, regularly precedes the chief <hi type="italic">factum</hi> ויּרני; see under Gen 1:2. Superficially understood, the expression 3a would be a platitude; the author means that the natural legal relation was also confirming itself as a moral one. It was a relation of many-sided love, according to 3a: he was esteemed of his mother - לפני, used of the reflex in the judgment, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.9">Gen 10:9</reference>, and of loving care, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">Gen 17:18</reference>, means this - as a tender child, and therefore tenderly to be protected (רך as <reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>), and as an only child, whether he were so in reality, or was only loved as if he were so. יחיד (Aq., Sym., Theod., μονογενής) may with reference to number also mean <hi type="italic">unice dilectus</hi> (lxx ἀγαπώμενος); cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.22.2">Gen 22:2</reference>, יחידך (where the lxx translate τὸν ἀγαπητόν, without therefore having ידידך before them). לפני is maintained by all the versions; לבני is not a variant.<note placement="foot">In some editions לבני is noted as Kerı̂ to לפני, but erroneously and contrary to the express evidence of the Masora, which affirms that there are two passages in which we ought to read not לפני, but לבני, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference> and Pro 4:3.</note> <div eID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> The instruction of the father begins with the jussive, which is pointed יתמך־<note placement="foot">The writing of -יתמך with the grave <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gaja</hi>) and <hi type="italic">Kametz-Chatuph</hi> (ǒ) is that of Ben Asher; on the other hand, יתמך־ with Cholem (ō) and the permanent <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> is that of Ben Naphtali; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 21a [under the verbal form 25], §30.</note> to distinguish it from יתמך־ on account of the ǒ. The lxx has incorrectly ἐρειδέτω, as if the word were יסמך; Symmachus has correctly κατεχέτω. The imper. וחיה is, as <reference osisRef="Prov.7.2">Pro 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>, more than ותחיה; the teacher seeks, along with the means, at the same time their object: Observe my commandments, and so become a partaker of life! The Syriac, however, adds תּורתיו כּאישׁון עיניך and my instruction as the apple of thine eye, a clause borrowed from Pro 7:2.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5-Prov.4.6">Pro 4:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen10666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> The exhortation of the father now specializes itself: 5 Get wisdom, get understanding;    Forget not and turn not from the words of my mouth. 6 Forsake her not, so shall she preserve thee;    Love her, so shall she keep thee. <div eID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> Wisdom and understanding are (5a) thought of as objects of merchandise (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">Pro 23:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">Pro 3:14</reference>), like the one pearl of great price, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">Mat 13:46</reference>, and the words of fatherly instruction (5b), accordingly, as offering this precious possession, or helping to the acquisition of it. One cannot indeed say correctly אל־תשׁכח מאמרי־פי, but אל־תשׁכח משּׁמר אמרי־פי (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.5">Psa 102:5</reference>); and in this sense אל־תּשׁכּח goes before, or also the accus. object, which in אל־תשכח the author has in his mind, may, since he continues with אל־תּט, now not any longer find expression as such. That the אמרי־פי are the means of acquiring wisdom is shown in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">Pro 4:6</reference>, where this continues to be the primary idea. The verse, consisting of only four words, ought to be divided by <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>;<note placement="foot">According to correct readings in codd. and older editions, ותשמרךּ has also indeed <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, and אהבה, <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> (with <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi>); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 47, §6; <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. §1, 2; and regarding the <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi>, see <hi type="italic">Liber Psalmorum Hebraicus</hi> by S. Baer, p. xii.</note> the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> (ו) in both halves of the verse introduces the <hi type="italic">apodosis imperativi</hi> (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Pro 3:9., and the <hi type="italic">apodosis prohibitivi</hi>, Pro 3:21.). The actual representation of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">Pro 4:5</reference>, becomes in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.6">Pro 4:6</reference> personal.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.7-Prov.4.9">Pro 4:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen10668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> Referring to <reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">Pro 4:5</reference>, the father further explains that wisdom begins with the striving after it, and that this striving is itself its fundamental beginning: 7 The beginning of wisdom is “Get wisdom,”    And with [um, at the price of] all thou hast gotten get understanding, 8 Esteem her, so shall she lift thee up;    She will bring thee honour if thou dost embrace her. 9 She will put on thine head a graceful garland,    She will bestow upon thee a glorious diadem. <div eID="gen10669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10670" type="x-p"/> In the motto of the book, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>, the author would say that the fear of Jahve is that from which all wisdom takes its origin. יראת יהוה (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>) is the subject, and as such it stands foremost. Here he means to say what the beginning of wisdom consists in. ראשׁית חכמה is the subject, and stands forth as such. The predicate may also be read קנה־חכמה (= קנות), after Pro 16:16. The beginning of wisdom is (consists in) the getting of wisdom; but the imperative קנה, which also Aq., Sym., Theod. (κτῆσαι), Jerome, Syr., Targ. express (the lxx leaves <reference osisRef="Prov.4.7">Pro 4:7</reference> untranslated), is supported by 7b. Hitzig, after Mercier, De Dieu, and Döderlein, translates the verse thus: “the highest thing is wisdom; get wisdom,” which Zöckler approves of; but the reasons which determine him to this rendering are subtleties: if the author had wished himself to be so understood, he ought at least to have written the words ראשׁית החכמה. But ראשׁית חכמה is a genitive of relation, as is to be expected from the relativity of the idea ראשׁית, and his intention is to say that the beginning of wisdom consists in the proposition קנה חכמה (cf. the similar formula, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ecc 12:13</reference>); this proposition is truly the <hi type="italic">lapis philosophorum</hi>, it contains all that is necessary in order to becoming wise. Therefore the Greek σοφία called itself modestly φιλοσοφία; for ἀρχὴ σὐτῆς the Book of Wisdom has, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.18">Pro 6:18</reference>, ἡ ἀληθεστάτη παιδείας ἐπιθυμία. In 7b the proposition is expressed which contains the <hi type="italic">specificum</hi> helping to wisdom. The בּ denotes price: give all for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">Mat 13:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mat 13:44</reference>); no price is too high, no sacrifice too great for it.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.13-Prov.4.14">Pro 4:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen10673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10674" type="x-p"/> The exhortations attracting by means of promises, now become warnings fitted to alarm: 13 Hold fast to instruction, let her not go;      Keep her, for she is thy life. 14 Into the path of the wicked enter not,      And walk not in the way of the evil 15 Avoid it, enter not into it;      Turn from it and pass away. 16 For they cannot sleep unless they do evil,      And they are deprived of sleep unless they bring others to ruin. 17 For they eat the bread of wickedness,      And they drink the wine of violence. <div eID="gen10674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10675" type="x-p"/> Elsewhere מוּסר means also self-discipline, or moral religious education, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.3">Pro 1:3</reference>; here discipline, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, parental educative counsel. תּרף is the segolated fut. apoc. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. (indic. תּרפּה) from tarp, cf. the imper. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הרף from harp. נצּרה is the imper. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> (not <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, as Aben Ezra thinks) with <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> <hi type="italic">dirimens</hi>; cf. the verbal substantive נצּרה <reference osisRef="Ps.141.3">Psa 141:3</reference>, with similar <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, after the form יקּהה, Gen 49:10. מוּסר (elsewhere always masc.) is here used in the fem. as the synonym of the name of wisdom: keep her (instruction), for she is thy life,<note placement="foot">Punctuate כּי היא; the <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi> represents the place of the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 9.</note><hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the life of thy life. In <reference osisRef="Prov.4.14">Pro 4:14</reference> the godless (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the root-idea of רשׁע under <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>) and the habitually wicked, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the vicious, stand in parallelism; בּוא and אשּׁר are related as entering and going on, <hi type="italic">ingressus</hi> and <hi type="italic">progressus</hi>. The verb אשׁר signifies, like ישׁר, to be straight, even, fortunate, whence אשׁר = Arab. yusâr, happiness, and to step straight out, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">Pro 9:6</reference>, of which meanings אשּׁר is partly the intensive, as here, partly the causative, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.19">Pro 23:19</reference> (elsewhere causative of the meaning, to be happy, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.13">Gen 30:13</reference>). The meaning <hi type="italic">progredi</hi> is not mediated by a supplementary צעדיו; the derivative אשׁוּר (אשּׁוּר), a step, shows that it is derived immediately from the root-idea of a movement in a straight line. Still less justifiable is the rendering by Schultens, <hi type="italic">ne vestigia imprimas in via malorum</hi>; for the Arab. âththr is denom. of ithr, אתר, the primitive verb roots of which, athr, אתר = אשׁר, are lost.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> <div eID="gen10676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10677" type="x-p"/> In the reason here given the perf. may stand in the conditional clauses as well as in Virgil’s <hi type="italic">Et si non aliqua nocuisses, mortuus esses</hi>; but the fut., as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>, denotes that they (the רעים and the רשׁעים) cannot sleep, and are deprived of their sleep, unless they are continually doing evil and bringing others into misery; the interruption of this course of conduct, which has become to them like a second nature, would be as the interruption of their diet, which makes them ill. For the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> יכשׁולוּ, which here must have the meaning of the person sinning (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference>), and would be feeble if used of the confirmed transgressors, the Kerı̂ rightly substitutes the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> יכשׁילוּ, which occurs also <reference osisRef="2Chr.25.8">2Ch 25:8</reference>, there without an object, in the meaning to cause to fall, as the contrast of עזר (to help).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> <div eID="gen10677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10678" type="x-p"/> The second כּי introduces the reason of their bodily welfare being conditioned by evil-doing. If the poet meant: they live on bread which consists in wickedness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, on wickedness as their bread, then in the parallel sentence he should have used the word חמס; the genitives are meant of the means of acquisition: they live on unrighteous gain, on bread and wine which they procure by wickedness and by all manner of violence or injustice. On the etymon of חמס (Arab. ḥamas, <hi type="italic">durum, asperum, vehementem esse</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Schultens; the plur. חמסים belongs to a more recent epoch (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.49">2Sa 22:49</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.18.49">Psa 18:49</reference>). The change in the tense represents the idea that they having eaten such bread, set forth such wine, and therewith wash it down.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18-Prov.4.19">Pro 4:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen10678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10679" type="x-p"/> The two ways that lie for his choice before the youth, are distinguished from one another as light is from darkness: 18 And the path of the just is like the brightness of the morning light,      Which shines more and more till the perfect day. 19 The way of the wicked is deep darkness,      They know not at what they stumble. <div eID="gen10679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10680" type="x-p"/> The Hebr. style is wont to conceal in its <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> (ו) diverse kinds of logical relations, but the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of 18a may suitably stand before 19a, where the discontinuance of this contrast of the two ways is unsuitable. The displacing of a <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> from its right position is not indeed without example (see under <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference>); but since <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> joins itself more easily than <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference> to <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> without missing a particle, thus it is more probable that the two verses are to be transposed, than that the ו of וארח (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>) is to be prefixed to דּרך (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference>). Sinning, says <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference>, has become to the godless as a second nature, so that they cannot sleep without it; they must continually be sinning, adds <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference>, for thus and not otherwise do they gain for themselves their daily bread. With reference to this fearful self-perversion to which wickedness has become a necessity and a condition of life, the poet further says that the way of the godless is כּאפלה,<note placement="foot">In good MSS and printed copies the כ has the <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, as Kimchi states the rule in <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 45a: כל כּאפלה פתח, כל כּאבנים פתח.</note> as deep darkness, as the entire absence of light: it cannot be otherwise than that they fall, but they do not at all know whereat they fall, for they do not at all know wickedness as such, and have no apprehension of the punishment which from an inward necessity it brings along with it; on the contrary, the path of the just is in constantly increasing light - the light of knowledge, and the light of true happiness which is given<note placement="foot">Hitzig inverts the order of <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pro 4:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference>, and connects the כּי of 16a immediately with <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> (for the way of the wicked...). He moreover regards <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">Pro 4:17</reference> as an interpolation, and explains <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> as a gloss transforming the text of Pro 4:19. “That the wicked commit wickedness,” says Hitzig, “is indeed certain (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference>), and the warning of <reference osisRef="Prov.4.15">Pro 4:15</reference> ought not to derive its motive from their energy in sinning.” But the warning against the way of the wicked is founded not on their energy in sinning, but on their bondage to sin: their sleep, their food and drink - their life both when they sleep and when they wake - is conditioned by sin and is penetrated by sin. This foundation of the warning furnishes what is needed, and is in nothing open to objection. And that in <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> לא ירעוּ and לא ידעוּ, יכשׁולוּ and יכּשׁלוּ, נגזלה and כּאפלה seem to be alike, does not prove that <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pro 4:16</reference> originated as a parallel text from <reference osisRef="Prov.4.19">Pro 4:19</reference> - in the one verse as in the other the thoughts are original.</note> in and with knowledge. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.4.20-Prov.4.22">Pro 4:20-22</reference> <div eID="gen10680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10681" type="x-p"/> The paternal admonition now takes a new departure: 20 My son, attend unto my words,      Incline thine ear to my sayings. 21 Let them not depart from thine eyes;      Keep them in the midst of thine heart. 22 For they are life to all who get possession of them,      And health to their whole body. <div eID="gen10681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10682" type="x-p"/> Regarding the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הלּין (for הלין), <reference osisRef="Prov.4.21">Pro 4:21</reference>, formed after the Chaldee manner like הלּין, הנּיח, הסּיג, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Gesenius, §72, 9; - Ewald, §114, c, gives to it the meaning of “to mock,” for he interchanges it with הלין, instead of the meaning to take away, <hi type="italic">efficere ut recedat</hi> (cf. under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.15">Pro 2:15</reference>). This supposed causative meaning it has also here: may they = may one (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Prov.2.22">Pro 2:22</reference>) not remove them from thine eyes; the object is (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.20">Pro 4:20</reference>) the words of the paternal admonition. Hitzig, indeed, observes that “the accusative is not supplied;” but with greater right it is to be remarked that ילּיזוּ (fut. <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. of לוּז) and ילוּזוּ (fut. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of <hi type="italic">id</hi>.) are not one and the same, and the less so as הלּיז occurs, but the masoretical and grammatical authorities (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Kimchi) demand ילּיזוּ. The plur. למצאיהם is continued, 22b, in the sing., for that which is said refers to each one of the many (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.28">Pro 3:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">Pro 3:35</reference>). מצא is fundamentally an active conception, like our “<hi type="italic">finden</hi>,” to find; it means to attain, to produce, to procure, etc. מרפּא means, according as the מ is understood of the “that = <hi type="italic">ut</hi>” of the action or of the “what” of its performance, either health or the means of health; here, like רפאוּת, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, not with the underlying conception of sickness, but of the fluctuations connected with the bodily life of man, which make needful not only a continual strengthening of it, but also its being again and again restored. Nothing preserves soul and body in a healthier state than when we always keep before our eyes and carry in our hearts the good doctrines; they give to us true guidance on the way of life: “Godliness has the promise of this life, and of that which is to come.” 1Ti 4:8.
